title: The Art of Ambiguous Narration
text:
Free indirect discourse, a technique perfected in the novels of Jane Austen, allows the narrator to slip into a character's thoughts without the explicit markers of direct speech. The result is a curious ambiguity, in which the reader cannot always tell whether a sentence belongs to the narrator's voice or to the character's own consciousness. Critics have long debated whether this blending is a sign of irony or of sympathy. Either way, it gives the novel a fluid perspective that shifts with remarkable ease.

Such ambiguity is not merely decorative. In Emma, for instance, the heroine's misjudgements are often presented in a voice that seems to endorse them, so that the reader must gradually learn to distrust both the narrator and the protagonist. This demands an active, almost forensic attention from the reader. Modern commentators therefore tend to regard Austen not as a writer of gentle comedy but as a meticulous analyst of self-deception.

questions.text: According to the passage, what does free indirect discourse allow the narrator to do?
options: Slip into a character's thoughts without explicit markers of direct speech
Address the reader directly in every chapter
Replace the characters' dialogue with summaries
Reveal the ending of the novel in advance

questions.text: In which novel are the heroine's misjudgements presented in a voice that seems to endorse them?
What can be inferred about the reader's experience of Austen's narration?
options: The reader must work actively to interpret the text
The reader can accept every statement at face value
The reader is told exactly what to think
The reader can safely ignore the narrator

questions.text: Why do modern commentators, according to the passage, regard Austen as more than a writer of gentle comedy?
options: Her narration exposes characters' self-deception with precision
She wrote only tragedies in her later years
Her novels were rejected by critics of her time
She invented free indirect discourse for her own use alone

to publicly approve of or support something

paragraph_translations: O discurso indireto livre, técnica aperfeiçoada nos romances de Jane Austen, permite que o narrador deslize para os pensamentos de uma personagem sem os marcadores explícitos da fala direta. O resultado é uma curiosa ambiguidade, na qual o leitor nem sempre consegue saber se uma frase pertence à voz do narrador ou à consciência da personagem. Os críticos debatem há muito se essa mescla é sinal de ironia ou de simpatia. De qualquer modo, ela confere ao romance uma perspectiva fluida que se desloca com notável facilidade.

Tal ambiguidade não é meramente decorativa. Em Emma, por exemplo, os equívocos da heroína são apresentados numa voz que parece endossá-los, de modo que o leitor deve aprender, aos poucos, a desconfiar tanto do narrador quanto da protagonista. Isso exige uma atenção ativa, quase forense, por parte do leitor. Por isso, comentadores modernos tendem a ver Austen não como autora de comédia leve, mas como uma analista meticulosa do autoengano.
